slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1960 and 1970 censuses interpolated to November 1964; men 21+ (18+ in Georgia and Kentucky, 19+ in Alaska, 20+ in Hawaii) outside the eleven Southern states, in the 50 states and DC (first presidential vote in DC, Twenty-third Amendment); calibrated to certified 1964 returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1960 and 1970 censuses interpolated to November 1964; women 21+ (18+ in Georgia and Kentucky, 19+ in Alaska, 20+ in Hawaii) outside the eleven Southern states, in the 50 states and DC (first presidential vote in DC, Twenty-third Amendment); calibrated to certified 1964 returns.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1960 and 1970 censuses interpolated to November 1964; white adults (21+ (18+ in Georgia and Kentucky, 19+ in Alaska, 20+ in Hawaii)) in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults) (the Twenty-fourth Amendment ended poll taxes in federal elections in January 1964); calibrated to certified 1964 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1960 and 1970 censuses interpolated to November 1964; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; registration still held to well under half of Black adults by literacy tests, registrar discretion and intimidation (the Voting Rights Act came only in 1965). The shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1960 and 1970 censuses interpolated to November 1964; foreign-born white adults who were not naturalized citizens (aliens could not vote in any state).

whatIfs.label: Everyone Votes
whatIfs.detail: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
whatIfs.assumption: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1964.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1964 comes out as it did: Johnson wins, 486–52. The closest state was Arizona, which went to Goldwater by 1.0 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1960 census counts carried to 1964 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1964 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 44.4 million more adults vote. Arizona, Georgia, Louisiana flip, but Johnson still wins, 513–25. The closest call is South Carolina, which holds for Goldwater by 1.1 points. Goldwater wins in 0 of 100 draws.
assumptions: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1964.
howIGotThis: What changed: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
New voters borrow the behaviour of naturalized citizens of the same state and sex; Black voters outside the South.
The numbers: the 1960 census counts carried to 1964 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1964 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.
